title: BRICKSTORM Backdoor Investigation
description: Investigate unusual network behavior on a target system to determine the nature of unexpected outbound connections.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The target system has exhibited unusual network behavior, including unexpected outbound connections to unknown destinations. Your task is to investigate and determine the nature of this activity. This scenario involves a backdoor that communicates with a command and control (C2) server. The malware family, known as BRICKSTORM, is notorious for its persistence mechanisms using systemd services. BRICKSTORM typically establishes a connection to a C2 server to receive commands and exfiltrate data, making it a significant threat to system integrity and data security. You will need to find flags such as service names and file paths to complete this investigation.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have SSH access to the target system with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. The target system is named `target` and is part of the `192.168.50.0/24` network. To proceed to the next level, enter the word 'start'.
levels.local_content: You have SSH access to the target system with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. The target system is named `target` and is part of the `192.168.50.0/24` network. To proceed to the next level, enter the word 'start'.

levels.title: Investigate Unusual Network Connections
levels.content: Investigate the unusual network connections on the target system. What is the name of the systemd service (flag: service name) responsible for the unexpected outbound connections?
levels.solution: Check the systemd services and look for any that are not part of the standard system configuration. The service responsible for the unexpected outbound connections is the `lab-checkin.service` service.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Start by checking the systemd services to identify any unusual or non-standard services.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all active services and look for any that seem suspicious.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The suspicious service is likely named `lab-checkin.service`.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Determine how the suspicious service maintains persistence on the system. What is the path to the systemd service unit file (flag: file path) that ensures the suspicious service starts automatically?
levels.solution: Look for service unit files in the `/etc/systemd/system/` directory that are related to the suspicious service. The service unit file that ensures the suspicious service starts automatically is `lab-checkin.service`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Persistence mechanisms often involve service unit files in the `/etc/systemd/system/` directory.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Check the `/etc/systemd/system/` directory for any suspicious service unit files related to the `lab-checkin.service`.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The service unit file you are looking for is located at `/etc/systemd/system/lab-checkin.service`.

levels.title: Identify Executable File
levels.content: Identify the executable or file associated with the suspicious activity. What is the path to the executable file (flag: file path) used by the suspicious service?
levels.solution: Check the service unit file for the suspicious service to find the path to the executable.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Review the service unit file to understand how the service is configured and what executable it uses.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for the `ExecStart` directive in the service unit file to find the path to the executable.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The executable file is located at `/usr/local/bin/lab-checkin.sh`.
